prompt:
Let $n$ be a positive integer. Let $a_1,a_2,\dots,a_n$ be real numbers such that $-1\le a_i\le1$ for all $1\le i\le n$, and let $b_1,b_2,\dots,b_n$ be real numbers such that $-1\le b_i\le1$ for all $1\le i\le n$. Prove that
$$\left|\prod_{i=1}^na_i-\prod_{i=1}^nb_i\right|\le\sum_{i=1}^n|a_i-b_i|.$$
answer: Telescope through the hybrid products $P_k=a_1\cdots a_kb_{k+1}\cdots b_n$; each step changes the product by at most $|a_k-b_k|$.

solutions.title: Telescoping hybrids
solutions.body:
For $0\le k\le n$ let $P_k=a_1\cdots a_k\,b_{k+1}\cdots b_n$, so $P_n=\prod a_i$ and $P_0=\prod b_i$. For $1\le k\le n$,
$$P_k-P_{k-1}=(a_k-b_k)\prod_{i<k}a_i\prod_{j>k}b_j,$$
and since all $|a_i|,|b_j|\le1$, we get $|P_k-P_{k-1}|\le|a_k-b_k|$. By the triangle inequality,
$$\left|\prod a_i-\prod b_i\right|=\left|\sum_{k=1}^n(P_k-P_{k-1})\right|\le\sum_{k=1}^n|P_k-P_{k-1}|\le\sum_{k=1}^n|a_k-b_k|.\ ∎$$

prompt: Say that a (nondegenerate) triangle is *funny* if it satisfies the following condition: the altitude, median, and angle bisector drawn from one of the vertices divide the triangle into $4$ non-overlapping triangles whose areas form (in some order) a $4$-term arithmetic sequence. (One of these $4$ triangles is allowed to be degenerate.) Find with proof all funny triangles.
answer: Exactly the right triangles whose sides are in ratio $1:\sqrt3:2$ or $1:2\sqrt6:5$ (cevians drawn from the vertex $A$ opposite a leg, with the right angle at $B$).

solutions.title: Bases form an arithmetic progression
solutions.body:
Let the cevians come from $A$: altitude $AH$, bisector $AL$, median $AM$, with $b=AC$, $c=AB$.

**$b\ne c$.** If $b=c$ then $H=L=M$, and the four areas are $0,0,s,s$ (with $s>0$), which is not an arithmetic progression. So assume $c<b$.

**Order of the points.** Since $c<b$, $\angle C<\angle B$, so $\angle BAH=90^\circ-\angle B<90^\circ-\angle C=\angle CAH$ and $H$ is closer to $B$ than $L$ is (the bisector splits $\angle A$ evenly while $AH$ makes the smaller angle with $AB$). By the angle bisector theorem $\frac{BL}{LC}=\frac cb<1$, so $L$ is closer to $B$ than the midpoint $M$ is. Thus the points occur in the order $B,H,L,M,C$ (with $H$ possibly equal to $B$).

**Arithmetic progression.** The four triangles $ABH,AHL,ALM,AMC$ share the height $AH$, so their areas are proportional to the bases $BH,HL,LM,MC$. These four lengths form, in some order, $x,x+d,x+2d,x+3d$ with $x\ge0$, $d\ge0$. Since $MC=BM=BH+HL+LM$, the base $MC$ is the largest, so $MC=x+3d$ and the other three are $x,x+d,x+2d$ in some order, with sum $3x+3d$. Hence $3x+3d=x+3d$, so $x=0$.

Thus one base is $0$ and then $d>0$. As $HL>0$, $LM>0$, $MC>0$, it must be $BH=0$: $H=B$, so $\angle B=90^\circ$. The remaining bases $BL,LM$ are $d$ and $2d$ in some order, $MC=3d$, and $a=BC=6d$.

**Case $BL=d$, $LM=2d$.** Then $LC=5d$ and by the angle bisector theorem $\frac bc=\frac{LC}{BL}=5$. So $b=5c$, $a=\sqrt{b^2-c^2}=2\sqrt6\,c$; the sides are in ratio $1:2\sqrt6:5$.

**Case $BL=2d$, $LM=d$.** Then $LC=4d$, $\frac bc=2$, $a=\sqrt3c$; the sides are in ratio $1:\sqrt3:2$ (a $30$-$60$-$90$ triangle).

**Converse.** In a triangle with $\angle B=90^\circ$ we have $H=B$, $BM=\frac a2$, $BL=\frac{ac}{b+c}$. For $b=5c$: $BL=\frac a6$ and the bases are $0,\frac a6,\frac a3,\frac a2$, an arithmetic progression. For $b=2c$: $BL=\frac a3$, bases $0,\frac a3,\frac a6,\frac a2$, which in order $0,\frac a6,\frac a3,\frac a2$ form an arithmetic progression. So both families are funny.

**Answer:** the funny triangles are exactly the right triangles with side lengths in ratio $1:\sqrt3:2$ or $1:2\sqrt6:5$. ∎

prompt: $10000$ nonzero digits are written in a $100$-by-$100$ table, one digit per cell. From left to right, each row forms a $100$-digit integer. From top to bottom, each column forms a $100$-digit integer. So the rows and columns form $200$ integers (each with $100$ digits), not necessarily distinct. Prove that if at least $199$ of these $200$ numbers are divisible by $2013$, then all of them are divisible by $2013$.
answer: Weight the entry in row $i$, column $j$ (counted from the bottom/right) by $10^{i+j}$: then $\sum_i10^iR_i=\sum_j10^jC_j$; and $\gcd(10,2013)=1$.

solutions.title: Double counting with weights
solutions.body:
Number the rows $i=0,\dots,99$ from the bottom and the columns $j=0,\dots,99$ from the right; let $a_{ij}$ be the digit in row $i$, column $j$. The row number is $R_i=\sum_j10^ja_{ij}$ and the column number is $C_j=\sum_i10^ia_{ij}$.

Compute $\sum_{i,j}10^{i+j}a_{ij}$ in two ways:
$$\sum_{i}10^{i}R_i=\sum_{i,j}10^{i+j}a_{ij}=\sum_j10^{j}C_j.$$
Suppose all but one of the $200$ numbers are divisible by $2013$. Then in the equation $\sum_i10^iR_i=\sum_j10^jC_j$ all terms are divisible by $2013$ except at most one term, $10^tX$, where $X$ is the remaining number. Hence $2013\mid10^tX$. Since $2013=3\cdot11\cdot61$ is coprime to $10$, $2013\mid X$. So all $200$ numbers are divisible by $2013$. ∎

prompt: We are given a finite set of segments of the same line. Prove that we can color each segment red or blue such that, for each point $p$ on the line, the number of red segments containing $p$ differs from the number of blue segments containing $p$ by at most $1$.
answer: Build a graph on the endpoints with 'interval' edges and 'consecutive' edges (pair up sorted endpoints); it is a union of even cycles, so 2-colourable. Colour each segment by the colour of its left endpoint.

solutions.title: Two-colouring a graph of endpoints
solutions.body:
Treat the segments as closed intervals $[a_i,b_i]$, $i=1,\dots,n$, and use colours $\pm1$. We need $\left|\sum_{i:\,a_i\le p\le b_i}x_i\right|\le1$ for every real $p$, where $x_i$ is the colour of interval $i$.

**The graph.** Take the $2n$ endpoints $a_1,b_1,\dots,a_n,b_n$ as distinct vertices. List them in non-decreasing order of value, placing left endpoints ($a$'s) before right endpoints ($b$'s) among equal values (otherwise arbitrary). Add two kinds of edges: *interval edges* $a_ib_i$, and *consecutive edges* joining the 1st and 2nd points of the list, the 3rd and 4th, etc. Each vertex lies on exactly one edge of each kind, so every component is a cycle whose edges alternate between the two kinds; thus every cycle is even (a double edge counts as a $2$-cycle). Hence the graph can be coloured with $\pm1$ so that adjacent vertices get opposite colours.

**The colouring.** Let $x_i$ be the colour of $a_i$. Then the colour of $b_i$ is $-x_i$. Colour interval $i$ with $x_i$.

**Check.** Fix $p$. The intervals containing $p$ are those with $a_i\le p$ minus those with $b_i<p$ (an interval with $b_i<p$ has $a_i\le b_i<p$). So
$$\sum_{a_i\le p\le b_i}x_i=\sum_{a_i\le p}x_i-\sum_{b_i<p}x_i=\sum_{a_i\le p}(\text{colour of }a_i)+\sum_{b_i<p}(\text{colour of }b_i).$$
The set of points $\{a_i\le p\}\cup\{b_i<p\}$ is an initial segment of our sorted list (all points with value $<p$, together with the $a$'s of value $p$, which come before the $b$'s of value $p$). Cutting this initial segment into consecutive pairs $(1,2),(3,4),\dots$, each pair has opposite colours and contributes $0$; at most one point is left over. So the sum has absolute value at most $1$. ∎
